blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this subject, so this part was written for the site, as of October 2026. Frontend libraries change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on a detail.
Test what users do, not how components work inside. A test that survives a refactor is a good test.

blocks.code:
flowchart TB
  A[A few end-to-end tests: Playwright, main journeys] --> B[Many component and integration tests: Testing Library + MSW]
  B --> C[Unit tests: Vitest, for pure logic]
  D[Static checks: TypeScript and ESLint] --> C
blocks.title: A practical test mix

blocks.text:
| Level | Test | Tool | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Static | Types and common mistakes | TypeScript, ESLint | Instant |
| Unit | Reducers, formatters, utilities | Vitest | Milliseconds |
| Component | A screen with mocked network | Testing Library, MSW | Fast |
| End to end | A real browser against a real app | Playwright | Slow |

| Worth testing | Not worth testing |
|---|---|
| User journeys and business rules | Implementation details |
| Form validation and error states | That React renders a prop |
| Edge cases: empty, loading, failure | Third-party libraries |
| Complex reducers and helpers | Exact styling |

blocks.text: ### Unit testing logic

blocks.title: A reducer test needs no React
Key points
blocks.text:
- Test behaviour rather than internals
- Most tests belong in the middle
- Pure logic is cheapest to test
- Types catch a whole class of bugs
### Query as a user would

blocks.title: A form test

blocks.text:
| Query priority | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `getByRole` | `button`, with name "Save" | Best: also checks accessibility |
| `getByLabelText` | Form fields | |
| `getByText` | Non-interactive content | |
| `getByTestId` | Last resort | Users can't see test IDs |

| Prefix | Not found | Waits | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `getBy` | Throws | No | Should be there now |
| `queryBy` | Returns null | No | Assert absence |
| `findBy` | Rejects after a timeout | Yes | Appears later |

If `getByRole` can't find your button, your markup may be inaccessible, and the test has done you a favour.

### Mocking the network with MSW

Mock Service Worker intercepts requests at the network level, so that your real `fetch` code runs, and no `api` module mocks are needed.

blocks.title: src/test/server.ts
Testing all the states

blocks.text:
Use a new `QueryClient` per test, so that cached data doesn't leak between tests, and turn off retries so that failure tests finish quickly.

### Testing hooks

blocks.title: renderHook

blocks.text:
### Common problems

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "not wrapped in act" warning | An update after the test's checks | Await with `findBy` or `waitFor` |
| Unable to find an element | Not there yet | Use `findBy` |
| Tests pass alone, fail together | Shared state | New client; reset handlers |
| Router errors | No router in the test | Wrap in `MemoryRouter` |
| Test checks a class name | Implementation detail | Check behaviour or accessible state |

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Query by role and label
- Use user-event rather than fireEvent
- MSW mocks at the network level
- New QueryClient per test
Component tests can't prove the whole system works. A few end-to-end tests cover the journeys that matter most: sign in, checkout and the main workflow.

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Start PostgreSQL in a container] --> B[Start Spring Boot with test data]
  B --> C[Serve the React build]
  C --> D[Playwright runs tests]
  D --> E[Upload traces on failure]
blocks.title: End-to-end in CI

blocks.text:
Each test should create its own data, through the API where possible, so that tests can run in parallel and don't depend on order.

### Keeping tests reliable

| Do | Avoid |
|---|---|
| Use roles and labels | Fragile CSS selectors |
| Auto-waiting assertions | Fixed sleeps |
| Create data per test | Shared accounts changing state |
| Keep the suite small | Testing every validation here |
| Mock third parties, such as payment | Calling real external services |

### Contract tests

Frontend and backend can each pass their own tests, and still disagree. Generating types from OpenAPI, as Part 3 shows, or contract testing with a tool such as Pact, catches this mismatch early.

### Accessibility and visual testing

`@axe-core/playwright` scans pages for accessibility violations, and Playwright can compare screenshots to catch visual regressions. Keep visual checks few, as they're sensitive to small changes.

**"How do you test a React app?"** TypeScript and ESLint first. Unit tests for pure logic. Most tests are component tests with Testing Library and MSW, covering loading, empty and error states. A few Playwright tests cover key journeys against the real backend.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- A few end-to-end tests for key journeys
- Rely on auto-waiting
- Each test creates its own data
- Don't call real third parties

blocks.text: ### Timers

blocks.title: Fake timers with user-event

blocks.text:
Without `advanceTimers`, user-event's own internal delays wait on the fake clock, and the test hangs. It's a common cause of mysterious timeouts.

### Things jsdom doesn't have

jsdom isn't a real browser: it has no layout, so sizes are 0. Provide stubs in your setup file for APIs such as `IntersectionObserver`, `matchMedia` and `ResizeObserver`.

blocks.title: A stub in setup.ts

blocks.text: If a test depends on real layout, such as virtualisation, use Playwright instead.

Submitting a React Router `<Form>` in a jsdom test can fail with "Expected init.body to be an instance of URLSearchParams". jsdom has its own `URLSearchParams`, which Node's `Request` rejects. The app is fine: the mismatch exists only in the test environment. Test the action as a plain function, or cover it with Playwright.

blocks.text: ### Accessible states as assertions

blocks.title: Testing what users perceive
Key points
blocks.text:
- Keep providers in one helper
- Assert what was sent, and what's shown
- Delay responses to see loading
- jsdom has no layout

### Writing the test first

TDD works well for behaviour with clear rules. Let's add a discount field.

blocks.title: 1. Describe the behaviour: this fails, as there's no field yet
2. Make it pass in the simplest way

blocks.text:
**3. Next test:** an invalid code shows an error. It fails, as `res.ok` isn't checked yet, which you then add. Each test drives the next piece of code, and each failure case gets remembered. Then refactor with the tests protecting you.

### What coverage means

blocks.code: npx vitest run --coverage
blocks.title: Coverage with Vitest

blocks.text:
Coverage shows which lines ran, but not whether anything was checked. A test that renders a component with no assertions gives high coverage and no protection. Use it to find **untested areas**, not as a target to hit. A sensible team watches the trend, and looks closely at critical paths.

| Metric says | Doesn't say |
|---|---|
| This line ran | The result was checked |
| This branch was taken | Every input is right |

### Mutation testing

A mutation tool such as Stryker changes your code, for example `>` to `>=`, and sees if tests fail. Tests that keep passing are weak. It's slow, so run it occasionally on critical logic.

### Tests that hurt

| Smell | Problem | Better |
|---|---|---|
| Snapshot of a whole page | Fails on any change; gets blindly updated | Assert specific behaviour |
| Mocking everything | Tests only your mocks | Mock the network alone |
| Testing hook internals | Breaks on refactor | Test through the UI |
| Sleeping | Slow and flaky | `findBy`, `waitFor` |
| Order dependence | Random failures | Isolated setup |
| Huge shared fixtures | Hard to read | Small factories per test |

### Storybook

Storybook renders components alone, in each state, without running your app. It's useful as living documentation for design systems, and it makes states that are hard to reach, such as errors, simple to see. It can also run accessibility checks and interaction tests.

blocks.title: A story for each state

blocks.text: ### A CI order

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Lint and types] --> B[Unit and component tests]
  B --> C[Build]
  C --> D[End-to-end tests]
  D --> E[Deploy]
blocks.title: Fast checks first

blocks.text: Fast checks run first, so failures show up in seconds. Run the end-to-end tests on main branches and before releases, if they're too slow for every push.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Tests can drive design
- Coverage finds gaps, not quality
- Mock only at the network
- Run fast checks first
#### A testing strategy

items.question: Why avoid testing a component's internal state?
items.answer: It breaks on refactoring even when behaviour is the same, and it doesn't prove users can do anything.

items.question: Why do reducers make testing easier?
items.answer: They're pure functions, so no rendering or mocks are needed.

blocks.text: #### Component tests with Testing Library

items.question: Why prefer getByRole to a test ID?
items.answer: It finds elements as users and assistive technology do, and fails if the markup isn't accessible.

items.question: getBy, queryBy or findBy: which do you use to check that something is absent?
items.answer: `queryBy`, as it returns null rather than throwing.

items.question: Why mock at the network level rather than mocking your API module?
items.answer: Your real client code runs, including error handling, and tests survive refactoring.

blocks.text: #### End-to-end tests with Playwright

items.question: Why not test everything end to end?
items.answer: They're slow and can be brittle. Keep them for main journeys, and use faster tests for detail.

items.question: A Playwright test sometimes fails, and passes on retry. What do you look for?
items.answer: Shared data, fixed sleeps, or order dependence. Use its trace to see what happened.

blocks.text: #### Testing recipes

items.question: A fake-timer test with user-event times out. What's missing?
items.answer: Pass `advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime` to `userEvent.setup`, so that its delays advance.

items.question: Why can't jsdom test a virtualised list well?
items.answer: It has no layout, so element sizes are zero. Use a real browser test.

items.question: How do you assert what a form sent?
items.answer: Capture the request body in the MSW handler, and assert on it.

blocks.text: #### Test-driven React, coverage and quality

items.question: A file has 100% coverage. Is it well tested?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Lines ran, but nothing may have been asserted. Check that tests fail when the code breaks.

items.question: Why avoid large snapshots?
items.answer: They fail on any change, and people update them without reading, so bugs slip through.

items.question: What does a mutation tool reveal?
items.answer: Whether tests really detect changes in logic.
